# Native system architecture

This chapter describes the native implementation: `SmartAccount`, a protocol
service with a small, explicit authorization boundary. Its wire contract is the
module protocol in [SA-MODULE-PROTOCOL.md](SA-MODULE-PROTOCOL.md), pinned by the
[v4.1 IDL](proposals/smartaccount-v4.1.idl.json). The [SDK](SDK.md) and the
[workspace](GUIDE.md) consume that contract; neither can grant authority the native
contract refuses. The profile is a draft until the Neo proposal and activation process
is complete.

The [account workspace](GUIDE.md) covers setup, backups,
the authority and timing matrix, and recovery decisions.

## Account identity and authority

An account has a stable account ID and a derived verification-script address.
The address holds assets without deploying one wallet contract per user. Custody
and recovery addresses are authorities, not the account's identity. Changing
custody does not change the funding address or reset operation nonces.

| Role | Authority |
| --- | --- |
| Custody | Witness authorization of ordinary UserOps when no validator is installed; immediate `freezeAccount` and `revokeModuleCredentials`; never direct installation, configuration or unfreeze |
| Recovery | RecoveryModule policy (guardians, delay) and the mature `resetAccount` landing |
| Verifier | Authorization of the exact operation; bound to an admitted module and its current configuration |
| Hook | Policy checks before and after target execution |
| Fee payer | Signs and pays for the complete transaction, including fees and expiry |
| RPC, SDK, UI | Discovery, construction, simulation and submission; no independent authority |

Recovery advances an authority epoch, the configuration nonce and the control
revision, replaces custody, removes every module instance and every nonce channel
record, and restores the built-in authorization defaults. It does not invoke the
old modules. Account identity, the module-id allocator and the derived funding
address remain intact, and the account returns to Active. Unfreezing keeps its
own governed path; recovery is not a silent unfreeze.

A guardian roster and guardian-initiated emergency containment are RecoveryModule
policy, not native authority. Choose an accepted Neo wallet authority controlled
independently from custody and keep both wallet backups. Freeze itself is the
immediate custody entry; unfreezing requires a matured GovernanceModule intent.
If a guardian key is lost while the account is Frozen, no native entry bypasses
the governed unfreeze; the module's own policy is the only replacement path.

Freeze takes effect when its transaction executes. Pending governance intents
live in GovernanceModule, not in native records; the core simply refuses governed
writes while the account is Frozen. For emergency containment followed by
recovery, freeze first, confirm the resulting state, then start a new recovery
proposal. Proposing recovery alone does not freeze the account. A successful
counter-advancing transition also invalidates pending configuration, so every
subsequent action must reload current state.

Module replacement, configuration, built-in authorization changes and unfreeze
are GovernanceModule intents: custody proposes, the module enforces the 24-hour
delay and 7-day window, and the matured intent commits through `configureModule`
or `applyConfigurationActions`. The native core holds no intent record and has no
cancellation entry; cancellation is GovernanceModule state. Module replacement still
checks code pins and old-module cleanup. The SDK's policy cancellation builds a
complete transaction script that reads and serializes the selected pending call,
asserts equality with reviewed bytes, and only then invokes the module cancellation
entry. It faults on changed or missing content without cancelling a replacement.
Exact-script signing is required; ordinary wallet invoke cannot express this guard.
An identical-byte re-proposal can still match, because the proposal has no unique
instance counter. See the [native account workspace](GUIDE.md#native-account-workspace).
Coordinate custody devices and inspect confirmed state after execution.

Supported native modules address storage by account ID and authority epoch.
Reinstalling the same module after recovery starts with empty policy state.
Normal module replacement still performs checked cleanup. The independent
recovery path handles broken or unavailable old modules.

## Execution and revocation

1. Discover the native contract on the explicitly selected network and verify
   its identity, ABI version, profile digest and activation.
2. Read current account state and the selected operation nonce channel. Build
   the exact target, method, typed arguments, deadline and nonce.
3. Bind authorization to network, native contract, account, authority epoch and
   configuration nonce inside the canonical 13-field operation. Execute with
   `executeUserOp(accountId, operation)`: one operation per call and per
   transaction script. There is no batch execution
   entry; the only batches are the salts of `createAccounts` (up to 64) and the
   actions of `applyConfigurationActions` (up to 16). No entry takes separate
   expected counters as arguments.
4. The proxy witness script calls `verify(accountId)`. The Verification trigger
   checks admissibility only: a proxy caller that is not the payer, an Active
   account, the proof that the transaction script is exactly one
   `executeUserOp` call for this account, the deadline, the authority epoch,
   the configuration nonce and nonce availability. The operation is read back
   from the script by fixed-tail byte comparison and literal decoding; no
   script is ever executed there. This binds transaction-witness authorization
   as well as operation signatures to the reviewed account state; an old
   signed transaction cannot survive a counter change merely because its
   nonce and block expiry remain valid.
5. Authorization happens once, inside `executeUserOp`: validate the operation,
   admit it, authorize it through the routed validator or the built-in custody
   signature, consume the nonce, run the pre-hooks forward, call the exact
   target and run the post-hooks in reverse. Callback arguments and results
   have independent copies so one callback cannot rewrite another callback's
   input. An invalid signature therefore passes the witness check and faults
   at execution: nothing changes and the fee is burned, so simulate before
   sending.
6. Verify the complete signed transaction against the node snapshot before
   broadcast, then read the actual transaction and application outcome.

The proxy witness grants the intended target frame only. It does not grant descendant calls access to assets.
The native account cannot be the transaction's fee payer: its operation proof
does not authorize arbitrary transaction fees.

## Supported policy modules

| Native module | Intended use |
| --- | --- |
| NeoWitnessValidator | Explicit Neo witness authorization with exact validator scopes |
| SessionKeyValidator | Expiring delegated keys and constrained operations |
| MultiSigValidator | Composite member validation; ThresholdPolicyModule holds the roster and threshold |
| WhitelistHook | Allowed targets and methods |
| DailyLimitHook | Bounded spending with measured token-balance changes |
| TokenRestrictedHook | Restricted token movement and policy checks |

Composite validation selects the first threshold of approving children in the
roster order held by ThresholdPolicyModule. The core lands each leaf approval
when the active composite instance calls `validateMember` and keeps that state
engine-local; it never reads the roster, the weights or the quorum. Only the
selected children receive post-execution authority and consume their policy
allowances. Supplying an additional valid signature does not select that child
once the quorum has been reached. The core checks the active code pins and
discards the operation state on completion or failure. Validation state never
carries into Application.

The composite instance compares its threshold, ordered roster and signer domains
before and after the selected children's post checks. Those children recheck
applicable current policy and account for the target result without repeating
SessionKey cryptographic verification. Receipt construction, copying and all
descendant calls run inside the declared `SystemFee` of the transaction; the
native core sets no per-callback budget.

The v4.1 profile admits at most 10 threshold members per policy and a quorum of
1–10, with a composite graph depth of one layer (no nesting, no cycles).
A standalone NeoWitnessValidator keeps its own ten-signer bound; the composite
limit does not reduce that separate capability. Supported combinations still
need to pass execution against the current fee policy and their actual module
bytecode.

Supported native P-256 keys use their standard Neo signature-account identity as
the canonical signer domain. The owning validator module strictly validates both
compressed and uncompressed encodings with `canonicalP256PublicKey` before
storing the compressed key; invalid curve points are rejected before any policy
write. P-256 verification is prehashed over a strict 32-byte digest and never
applies an implicit SHA-256.
Reusing one key as both a SessionKey and a
Neo signer therefore does not create two independent votes. This does not
prove that distinct keys belong to independent people or reveal who controls an
arbitrary verification script. Token policies likewise depend on the selected
tokens' behavior and balance queries. Exact profile metadata is an admission
compatibility check, not a proof that arbitrary third-party bytecode follows the
supported module implementations.

Governed configuration is delayed by 24 hours with a 7-day window inside
GovernanceModule; the recovery delay belongs to RecoveryModule and is fixed by
its own policy. Session expiry must leave time after activation. Delayed key
removal is not an emergency revoke button: custody freeze and
`revokeModuleCredentials` provide immediate containment, while RecoveryModule
provides the module-independent exit.

## Fees and user experience

An external payer signs the complete transaction and pays its fees without
acquiring account authority, after separate system, network and total fee
ceilings have been checked.

An included transaction whose Application ends in FAULT can still charge its
fee payer; reverted state changes do not refund transaction fees. A target
returning Boolean `false` is a business result, not itself a VM fault. Modules
and clients apply their own result checks, including the SDK's strict
Boolean-true requirement for `transfer`.

The native contract sets no per-call budget. The declared
`SystemFee` of the transaction is the only execution limit and is burned in
full, even when Application faults. Node simulation reports `gasconsumed`;
wallet and SDK builders take the system fee from the simulation of the built
transaction and never set it below the consumed gas.
Custom proxy verification and invocation scripts participate in network-fee
calculation. A fee increase after signing requires a new reviewed transaction.

Measured cost on the reference runtime (datoshi = 1e-8 GAS, Huyao enabled,
default Policy configuration):

| Case | GAS |
| --- | --- |
| Ordinary NEO transfer | 0.111 |
| Custodial single-key transfer | about 0.164 (12,866,237 execution engine + 3,548,066 network fee) |
| Module-routed 1-of-1 | about 0.217 |
| Threshold 2-of-3 | about 0.301 |
| Threshold 10-of-10 | about 0.593 |

Fee-policy changes and arbitrary third-party modules can change feasibility,
so a measured boundary vector establishes support only for its recorded
runtime and fee policy.

The workspace starts read-only and shows identity separately from the funding
address. Recovery descriptors contain public discovery information, not private
keys. Observed network, wallet, account or pending-intent changes invalidate
prepared reviews. Returned transaction IDs are submissions; exact transaction and receipt
readback are required before confirmation.
After a submission timeout, query the same transaction ID before preparing a
replacement. Successful simulation does not reserve a nonce or guarantee inclusion.

Ordinary wallet `invoke` APIs can handle supported single-authority management
calls. Proxy execution and multiple authorities require exact witness support;
the workspace exports a reviewable SDK recipe and exact script for those flows.
It does not disguise a script export as an executed transaction.

## Verification and activation

Source, contract bytecode, native runtime, RPC and client tests cover distinct
layers. Native module VM probes do not prove the native recovery state machine.
Mock browser tests do not prove a network transaction. Handwritten formal models
do not establish complete NeoVM/compiler refinement or cryptographic soundness.
See the [formal scope](engineering/VERIFICATION-AND-GATES.md) and
[open boundaries](SA-NATIVE-OPEN-BOUNDARIES.json).

Release evidence must identify the exact source and rebuilt artifacts, exercise
the complete signed transaction on the matching private runtime, verify state and
receipts after success and rejection, and retain reproducible build inputs.
Proposal acceptance, external review and network activation remain separate
decisions; the protocol has no network activation today.
